Romy Gonzalez seemed like a staple of the Boston Red Sox's offensive attack plan just a year ago. Now, with the playoffs looming, it's become difficult to see where he fits into the picture.
Having been demoted to Triple-A on Aug. 4, Gonzalez has been patiently waiting his turn. The Red Sox are used to having at least one right-handed bat on the roster who primarily gets his looks against left-handed pitchers, but Jahmai Jones has usurped that role from Gonzalez at least temporarily.
With 14 position players on the current active roster and likely 14 joining the Red Sox for the American League Wild Card Series in two weeks, there's an interesting conversation to have about Gonzalez now that the 30-year-old is having a hot month of September in Triple-A. Where will that conversation lead?
Is Gonzalez a legitimate threat to crack playoff roster?
Gonzalez batted near the top of the order for the Red Sox down the stretch last year whenever there was a lefty on the mound. But he also turned out to be battling a shoulder injury that necessitated surgery at the beginning of spring training and delayed his return to the majors until the end of June.
When he did make his season debut, Gonzalez recently admitted that he rushed his rehab, which might reasonably have thrown his swing out of whack against major league quality pitching. He went 12-for-65 with only one home run and a .572 OPS in his 19 major league games before his demotion.
“Where the team was at and all the injuries we had, it was my plan to kind of rush back and be up there,” Gonzalez said, via Christopher Smith of MassLive. “Obviously, hindsight’s 20/20.”
Now, with the Triple-A season coming to an end this weekend, Gonzalez has to know he might not make it back to the majors at all. But he's got the right attitude about the entire situation, seemingly.
“I’m ready whenever my name’s called,” Gonzalez said, per Smith.
If the Red Sox were going to put Gonzalez on the playoff roster, he'd likely have to displace either Connor Wong or Mickey Gasper. Nate Eaton, the current odd man out, should be replaced by Ceddanne Rafaela by the end of the week.

Dylan Cease's first season with the Toronto Blue Jays has been tremendous. He rewarded the front office's confidence after signing a lucrative contract this offseason.
Every team needs an ace. Cease assumed that role and took off with it. In the middle of a tight playoff race, the Blue Jays feel comfortable when the 30-year-old takes the mound. Since the All-Star break, Toronto is 7-4 when Cease pitches.
He's accomplished a lot of firsts this season, but could he add one more to the list?
Can Cease Win His First Cy Young?
Cease has been a strikeout machine since entering the league. He's eclipsed 200+ strikeouts for six consecutive seasons, and this year, he has a new career-high of 236 strikeouts and counting.
Now, Cease has his eyes set on his first American League Cy Young Award. In 2022, he was the runner-up to Justin Verlander, who won the award unanimously. In 2024, Cease finished fourth behind Paul Skenes (3), Zack Wheeler (2), and Chris Sale (1).
This could be his best chance yet. Jared Greenspan of MLB.com laid out the latest A.L. Cy Young poll. Cease finished second behind New York Yankees pitcher Cam Schlittler. Cease received 126 points and Schlittler received 160 points.
Comparing Cease and Schlittler
Schlittler: 14-6, 184.2 IP, 1.95 ERA, 0.90 WHIP, 228 SO, 44 BB
Cease: 11-5, 166.1 IP, 2.38 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 236 SO, 72 BB
While this may be Cease's best chance, those statistics suggest it will be tough to defeat Schlittler. The righty would have to put up incredible numbers over his final three or four starts, and Schlittler would need to go in the opposite direction.
The majority of Cease's advanced metrics rank in the 90th percentile or higher on Baseball Savant. His average exit velocity (85.6), whiff percentage (33.4), strikeout percentage (35.3), and hard-hit percentage (31.9) are some of the best in baseball this year.
Cease became the first Blue Jays pitcher to start the All-Star Game since Roy Halladay in 2009. It's incredible to think this was Cease's first All-Star nod. He would become the first Toronto pitcher to win the Cy Young Award. Two have won the award this century (Robbie Ray, 2021, and Roy Halladay, 2009).
Regardless of what happens, no one can take away the brilliant year Cease has had. The talent was always there. It was about finding the right organization to unlock it. The Blue Jays became the place where Cease could thrive.

Over the last few weeks, or so, it has seemed like pretty much every injury update for the Boston Red Sox has been positive.
Garrett Crochet has been throwing, Tanner Houck has been on a rehab assignment and even Curtis Mead has been playing catch, among others. While this is the case, the Red Sox gave a negative update on Wednesday. Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that reliever Justin Slaten is dealing with "degenerative changes in the flexor mass" and is likely done for the 2026 season.
"Slaten, we got ... he went and saw [Dr. Keith Meister] with our medical staff today and there's some degenerative changes in the flexor mass," Tracy said. "So he's going to be down. He's going to get a PRP injection and it's likely going to end his season. So, that's substantially different news, as far as these guys."
Bad News For Boston
This is a brutal blow for Slaten, and the Red Sox's bullpen in general. Slaten is one of the club's key high-leverage guys, but Boston hasn't had him on the mound since Aug. 12. He was initially placed on the Injured List due to right elbow inflammation. He actually started throwing, but he had to be shut down when the same "symptoms" that landed him on the Injured List popped up again.
Slaten had a 4.60 ERA in 36 appearances, but this doesn't tell the full story about why he's a big loss for Boston. In his final 17 appearances of the season, he had a 2.45 ERA and a 19-to-3 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 14 2/3 innings pitched. The first half of the season wasn't great for him, but he had turned things around and looked like the guy Boston hoped it would have out of the bullpen.
The Red Sox have just 11 games left in the 2026 regular season. Losing Slaten hurts Boston's playoff chances. On the bright side, the Red Sox's bullpen could still get better with Houck on a minor league rehab assignment and Garrett Crochet throwing as well. With Slaten likely out for the season, that's one less change Boston will have to make when building the playoff roster. Tyron Guerrero, Crochet, and Houck are all inching their way back. Boston will have to clear three spots to get these guys on the roster. That could be bad news for guys like Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, and Raymond Burgos, among others.
With Slaten likely not coming back, it's one less decision for Boston to make. Of course, it would be better if he were returning, but that isn't the case right now. Unfortunately, Red Sox fans have seemingly seen the last of Slaten for the 2026 season.

However, as we race toward October, it's time to start thinking about the postseason rotation, and we could see Bennett as the odd man out. Since August 1, the youngster has made seven starts and posted a 5.26 ERA.
The way he's performed over his last three starts has been interesting. On August 29, he twirled six scoreless innings against the New York Yankees while allowing just three hits. On September 3, he took the ball against the Baltimore Orioles and again went six deep, this time surrendering three runs. The two outings were basically the opposite ends of the spectrum of what we'd consider acceptable for a starter in the playoff rotation.
That Orioles start had a hidden concern, though. Bennett served up two homers, and it would prove prophetic for the next time he took the mound. That came on September 9 against the hapless Los Angeles Angels, who torched him for six earned runs over 5 1/3 innings. Bennett got taken deep three times in the affair and allowed eight balls to be hit over 100 miles per hour. His average exit velo for the start was a whopping 95.6 miles per hour.
At the same time, his chief competition for a spot in the playoff rotation, Ranger Suarez, might be rounding into form. The veteran struggled mightily in August after returning from the groin issue that landed him on the IL back in July, posting a 5.70 ERA for the month.
His lone start of September, though, was vintage Suarez, turning in seven shutout innings while allowing just five hits and a walk and generating a whole lot of soft contact.
If Ranger Suarez can prove he's back, he'll swipe Jake Bennett's spot in the Red Sox's playoff rotation
One start doesn't erase all the concern, but Suarez earned the second All-Star nod of his career thanks to his mostly stellar work in the first half. It's not unreasonable to assume that his string of uninspiring August performances was simply due to him knocking off the rust after being on the IL.
For Bennett, there's an added layer. With 105 innings already on his ledger in the majors and another 39 1/3 frames for the WooSox, he's well past what he's used to. In his first minor league season back in 2023, he pitched 63 frames. He missed the entire 2024 season after undergoing Tommy John surgery, and then came back to throw 75 1/3 innings last season.
Essentially, his 144 1/3 combined innings this year alone are greater than the 138 1/3 inning workload he's carried the last three years combined. He can say that the increased run hasn't affected him, but if the results on the field tell a different story, then that's the likely case.
There are two other factors to consider in the event of a proverbial tie. One, the Red Sox gave Suarez $130 million over the winter for a reason. Contracts shouldn't give an underperforming player a boost over a younger, cheaper option, but if all else is equal, it can help to be the deciding factor.
More importantly, Suarez is experienced in October. During his time with the Phillies, he's thrown 42 2/3 playoff innings and owns a 1.48 postseason ERA. That experience, and more importantly, excellence, matters, especially when it seems that the other option is running out of gas.

BOSTON — In a one-run game against the Kansas City Royals’ last homestand, Boston Red Sox shortstop Trevor Story hit a one-out double off the wall, raced to second base and dove head-first into the bag.
He flipped over on his back and held onto the bag, a safe call upheld after a Royals’ challenge.
Advertisement
The Red Sox eventually lost that game, but it was a small play that represented the bigger picture: Story was back. A diving, flipping play would have been hard to imagine for Story — or anyone watching him — earlier this season as he battled through a sports hernia injury that left him hitting .206 with a .547 OPS after 41 games.
Following surgery in May and a rehab that forced him to miss 93 games this season, Story has made a quiet but impactful return to the team.
He has hit safely in 13 of 14 games since returning, including Tuesday’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers. Since his activation Aug. 30 in New York, Story has started at shortstop in 14 of the team’s 15 games, going 19-for-56 (.339) with seven doubles and six RBIs. He’s hoping to make up for lost time.
“That was, ideally, the point of the surgery, to get it and come back and be able to do the things that I know I can do,” the 33-year-old said.
“It’s not invisible,” he said of the sports hernia’s effects. “I don’t think you would expect it to be after surgery and coming back. But it’s so much better than it was, and I’m getting stronger. So I’m happy about that. And I’m happy with the way my body has reacted. I wanted to be a part of this.”
It’s admittedly a small sample size since Story has returned, but if he had started slowly following his return, the calls for him to be replaced in the lineup would have grown louder. His replacements at shortstop — particularly a combination of Andruw Monasterio and Nick Sogard — filled in admirably during his absence as the Red Sox turned their season around. Story’s unproductive 10 rehab games with Triple-A Worcester, coupled with the rise of top prospect Franklin Arias, a shortstop raking at Triple A, created an echo chamber of angst about Story returning and underperforming.
So far, he hasn’t.
Advertisement
And he’s heard much of the criticism and frustration about his impending return. He understands it. His injury-riddled tenure in Boston has warranted that consternation. He missed much of 2024 recovering from extensive shoulder surgery and 2023 from elbow surgery. Of his five years in Boston, on a six-year, $140 million deal, he’s played only one healthy season.
Staying on the field has been his biggest bugaboo with the Red Sox. But the outside noise and frustration with his injuries motivated Story to prove he can still play.
“You see a lot of that stuff, but I really try to channel it into an energy in a way that I can use,” he said. “At the time, I wasn’t trying to pay much attention to it, but people would bring it to me, and I decided how I was going to look at it. I just tried to channel it into when I do come back, and it’s all about the playoffs, and it’s all about winning this thing at the end. That’s where I put my energy and focus.”
Roman Anthony, who missed 101 games with a torn finger ligament and rehabbed alongside Story, learned by watching the veteran handle the pressure.
“He’s unbelievable,” said Anthony. “Getting to go through this process with him. I was so happy for him. Every at-bat, he just continues to look better and better, and then to trust himself through all the noise.”
The return to the field has taken Story some effort, though. He arrives at the field roughly an hour before the team’s mandatory report time so that he can get on the trainer’s table to be stretched out for 30 to 45 minutes before his activation work in the gym, which leads into the team’s daily hitters’ meeting, then his workout before cage and field work.
“I’ve learned to kind of streamline it a little bit, and with the injury, (I) kind of know what (I) need,” he said. “In the gym, I’m just activating the right muscles, getting the core going, getting the hips right, adductor, glute med, the surrounding muscles from my surgery. So a lot of it is pre-hab. It’s mainly about the hips and getting the rotations right.”
Advertisement
The work has paid off early on. On Aug. 31, his first game back at Fenway Park in nearly four months, he cranked a base hit off the wall in the bottom of the ninth for a walk-off win.
This past Sunday, he padded a slim Red Sox lead against the Royals with a two-run single in the eighth. He’s hoping to carry this production through the rest of the season to prove he can be the player who hit .289 with an .827 OPS over the final four months of the 2025 season.
Despite missing so much of the year, the recent production since has helped him feel a part of the Red Sox’ run.
“As I’m sitting there watching the 15-game winning streak and starting to turn the whole season around, you watch it from the dugout and it’s like, ‘Man, this is something special,'” he said. “To be able to play a part and do my thing this late in the season means a lot to me.”

Red Sox Video
The Boston Red Sox are a near-lock for the second AL Wild Card spot. With just over 10 games left in the season, it’d take a whole mess of crazy for the Sox to move up or down. While it would be great to have a shot at moving up in the standings, their current situation will allow them to spend the final two weeks of the season freshening up their stalwarts, getting injury returnees back up to speed, and fixing Jarren Duran.
Duran hasn’t quite been the worst regular in Major League Baseball, but that’s damning with faint praise. He’s still an excellent baserunner and a plus fielder, but only Ezequiel Tovar has a lower wRC+ (51) among qualified hitters than Duran’s mark of 67. Despite his disintegrated noodle of a bat, he has racked up 578 plate appearances due to injuries and, presumably, a lack of better options, but that doesn’t make him a lost cause.
What makes Duran’s complete collapse at the plate so shocking is that he was a top-25 hitter by wRC+ only two seasons ago (132), and well above average just last season (112). While it’s safe to assume 2024 was a career year, he looked to have established himself as an above-average bat, and it’s not like all of his underlying metrics have cratered. If anything, many have improved.
He’s swinging the bat as fast as ever. His barrel rate is almost identical to the past two seasons. He’s pulling the ball in the air more. And while his in-zone contact rate is a career-low 84%, that’s a completely fair trade-off for what should be better power.
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
Now, you could argue that Duran didn’t need to change his approach from 2024, but given these figures, there’d be no reason to believe he had gone from one of the best hitters in baseball to almost the very worst. However, this chart doesn’t contain every last kernel of underlying data, and the one thing that has cratered for Duran is the most basic, fundamental skill of hitting—not chasing (f***ing) fastballs out of the zone.
Duran is running a wRC+ of 67 because his out-of-zone swing rate (O-Swing%) has ballooned to 34.5%, which is largely driven by a career-high O-Swing% of 36.8% against four-seam fastballs. Throughout his career, Duran’s production has largely followed his ability to lay off pitches out of the zone, but his inability to lay off four-seam fastballs (FA), to this degree, is new.
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
What makes his cratering performance against four-seamers so baffling is that it is exclusively down to swing decisions. His production when he makes contact is relatively unchanged, and he’s not whiffing a concerning amount in the zone. In fact, his zone contact rate against four-seamers is better than it was in 2024.
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
It’s not groundbreaking analysis to say that swinging at fastballs out of the zone is a bad idea, but it doesn’t necessarily doom a hitter to the abyss. However, Duran’s ability against four-seamers was a load-bearing trait, and it becoming a weakness has completely collapsed his profile because it has cost him the platoon advantage.
Unsurprisingly, Duran, a left-handed hitter, has made a career out of pulverizing right-handed pitching. His career wRC+ against righties is 114, compared to 72 against lefties. Splits like this are far from unusual, but what has happened to Duran in 2026 is. Over 410 plate appearances against righties, he has a wRC+ of 63. That’s the second-worst among qualified hitters, and it all stems from his struggles against four-seam fastballs.
This season, 37.3% of the pitches right-handers have thrown Duran have been four-seam fastballs, right in line with his career average of 38.7%. While four-seamers generally have more neutral platoon splits, historically, Duran absolutely feasted on right-handed four-seamers. Entering 2026, Duran had a +20.6 run value against right-handed four-seam fastballs, but he has somehow managed an absolutely preposterous, incomprehensible -13.1 run value in 2026.
The reason why Duran’s plate discipline has completely collapsed against four-seamers is a bit more of a mystery, but I think it starts with his increased desire to swing hard, lift, and pull. Over the past four seasons, as Duran’s swing speed has increased, he has hit the ball out in front a bit more.
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
None of this is particularly surprising and should be expected. A faster bat will make contact out in front more often, and bat speed increases throughout a swing. The two moving in tandem make all the sense in the world, but getting to this point could have come at a cost.
To sell out for swing speed and contact out in front, Duran likely has to get his operation started just a fraction of a second earlier, which means committing to pitches a tad earlier as well. The trickle-down effect is swinging at more pitches out of the zone, and in particular four-seam fastballs, which require the quickest decisions at the plate.
The Red Sox don’t need Jarren Duran to figure it out to make the playoffs, but getting him back to basics could unlock another level of the offense. With Duran producing at an average offensive level, suddenly the Sox could field an elite outfield defense of Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Duran, while letting Roman Anthony DH. However, for that dream arrangement to work, Duran needs to actually hit again, and that starts with laying off fastballs outside of the zone.

ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward.
The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come.
But while the Sox are amid a magic-number countdown to a playoff berth, they’ve done so without Anthony and Crochet for most of the year. Their season has been saved in no small part by players who have emerged from obscurity to play critical roles — with essential contributions coming from Andruw Monasterio, Anthony Seigler, Mickey Gasper, Tsung-Che Cheng, Jahmai Jones, Tyron Guerrero, and more.
“I don’t think anybody had that on the drawing board,” said interim manager Chad Tracy with a chuckle. “They were asked to play a lot, and they produced. And if they didn’t, we were in trouble. It’s a huge piece of the 2026 season, no question.”
Of course, while no one expected the outsized impact of players who began the year as big league backups or in Triple-A, the Sox also took considerable pains to build organizational depth through a variety of transactions.
Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.
“Every move and every decision matters,” said assistant general manager Mike Groopman, who oversees the team’s acquisitions group. “The big ones, whether it’s a larger free agent deal, [or] a larger, more high-profile trade, is naturally going to get a lot of attention.
“I don’t think this is unique to the Red Sox. There are 29 other teams that try to and do a very good job about caring about the ‘little’ things. But I think what we really try to reinforce is … that year over year, around the game, you see things that seem ‘little’ that end up being really impactful and big. [Deals that] seemed like small moves at the outset end up having a much, much larger impact commensurate with what would have been perceived at the time as a ‘larger’ move.”
Players who evolve from theoretical depth to become big league contributors excite numerous corners of an organization. The primary credit for those contributions, of course, belongs with a player, but they still often represent the combined efforts of personnel in scouting who identify the player’s potential contributions, player development personnel who help the player build on preexisting strengths and abilities in the minors, and big league staffers who help the players to perform at the game’s highest level.
Take Guerrero. After brief stints in the big leagues in 2018 and 2019, he’d become a journeyman, shuffling between organizations — and countries — but unable to forge a way back to the big leagues despite elite velocity.
But the Sox — who’d been interested in signing Guerrero before he pitched in the NPB in Japan in 2025 — remained intrigued, thanks in part to strong scouting recommendations from Kento Matsumoto in Japan and Manny Nanita in the Dominican Winter League. After they signed Guerrero to a minor league deal in the offseason, player development officials worked with him on some minor grip changes that unlocked significantly improved command with a sinker that regularly reached triple digits.
Guerrero’s dominance this year in Triple-A (0.92 ERA) essentially forced the Sox to call him up, and the 35-year-old emerged as a late-innings force from late June to late August (before shoulder fatigue led to a bad outing followed by a trip to the injured list), posting a 2.13 ERA over a 23-appearance stretch.
Again, the lion’s share of the credit goes to Guerrero for the work he did to fight his way back to the big leagues. But his emergence embodies the sort of under-the-radar acquisition that helped save the Sox’ season.
“The connection and integration between acquisition and development is really important,” said Groopman. “Guerrero and our [player development] group put a lot of time into [those changes] in the spring and the early season, to get him to a point where he was able to lock in some of these changes and unlock what was super obvious arm talent into something that was translating more consistently onto the major league mound.”
Of course, talent alone doesn’t dictate success once a depth player gets to the big leagues. They must also have the opportunity to contribute — and, in many cases, the freedom to fail while getting their bearings.
Tracy, who spent time with nearly all of this year’s depth contributors in Triple-A at the beginning of the year, has been mindful of creating an environment in which call-ups can contribute.
“I’m in the same boat [as them]. I want the freedom to go manage the game [as a first-time big league manager],” said Tracy. “I need to manage a game and feel like if I do something that doesn’t go right, it’s not the end of the world. If I feel that way, then I want the player to feel like, ‘Hey, if you go out there and play second base today and you make an error, move on to the next play.’
“If the culture becomes, ‘If I make a mistake, then all of a sudden I clam up and I get really tight,’ we’re going to have a problem. So you look at them and say, ‘You’re here for a reason: To go play your game. Don’t worry about making a mistake. Move on to the next pitch, next play.’ And they did that, and they were awesome.”

item.content:encoded:
Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out.
But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second.
Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers.
Nick Sogard hit a two-run home run to help get the Red Sox back into the game, but the offense otherwise couldn’t get anything going against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers bullpen, squandering bases loaded opportunities in the fifth and eighth innings.
Sandoval started strong by striking out the side in the first inning, but after sending down Jake Burger to start the second everything ground to a screeching halt. The right-hander allowed a pair of singles, served up a two-run double to Elias Diaz, and then walked back-to-back batters to load the bases for five-time All-Star Corey Seager.
It appeared for a moment like Sandoval might minimize the damage when he drew a pop fly to shallow left, but the ball drifted into no-man’s land and Trevor Story couldn’t make the catch, allowing two more runs to score and putting the Rangers up 4-0.
Sandoval ultimately needed 44 pitches to get through the second, blowing up his pitch count and ensuring a long evening for the Red Sox bullpen. He recorded two outs in the third and was lifted for Brayan Bello after allowing four runs over 2 2/3 innings.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Arlington postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
Four runs matches the largest deficit the Red Sox have overcome in a win this season, but the club didn’t need long to cut it in half. After Caleb Durbin reached on a one-out single in the top of the third, Sogard ripped a line drive off deGrom that cleared the right field fence for a two-run home run.
It was the fifth home run of the season for Sogard, all of which have come since Aug. 19. Prior to that the 29-year-old had never hit a homer over his first three seasons as a big leaguer.
That wound up being as close as Boston got.
The Red Sox could have tied the score or taken the lead with one swing in the fifth inning, but despite loading the bases without recording a hit the club couldn’t get a run across. Jarren Duran was hit by a pitch, Durbin reached on catcher’s interference and Mickey Gasper walked to bring up Adley Rutschman with two outs, but the catcher grounded out to short to keep it a 4-2 game.
Boston’s bullpen did its part to keep the Red Sox in the game. Bello tossed 1 2/3 perfect innings, Alec Gamboa threw one scoreless aided in large part by a brilliant double play turned by Sogard to end the fifth, and Wyatt Olds worked his way out of a runners-at-the-corners, two-out jam to escape the sixth. Jovani Moran entered with a man on in the seventh and got three quick outs, setting the table for one last Red Sox push in the eighth.
Jahmai Jones sparked the rally with a leadoff single, Willson Contreras drew a one-out walk, and after Wilyer Abreu grounded out to move the two runners into scoring position Story was intentionally walked to load the bases again.
Rather than have Duran face the left-hander Jacob Latz, Tracy pinch hit Andruw Monasterio, but the move didn’t pay off. Monasterio worked a full count and nearly went deep on a hard hit liner that landed just foul before striking out to leave them loaded again.
Boston went quietly in the top of the ninth, finishing the game 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position while stranding nine men on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up and we couldn’t do it tonight,” Tracy said.
Magic number still 5
In addition to keeping pace in the AL West race, the Rangers also jumped the Toronto Blue Jays to become the first team below the AL Wild Card cutline. As a result the Red Sox’s magic number remains five despite the Blue Jays’ 10-1 loss earlier in the night.
Boston (82-69) can clinch a playoff berth as early as Friday, and depending on how things play out in the AL Central the Red Sox could lock down the second Wild Card spot as soon as this weekend.
Houck scoreless with WooSox
Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery rehab) tossed a scoreless inning of relief in his latest rehab appearance with the WooSox on Tuesday. The right-hander entered the game in the seventh inning and allowed one walk, no hits and struck out three over 22 pitches.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 season has been, for the most part, an injury-plagued loss for Crochet, who made his first six starts before getting shut down with left shoulder inflammation that regressed when he made his first attempted comeback in late May.
But the beauty of all this is that Crochet can wash away the sour taste of missing most of the season by getting back as a reliever in time for the most important games.
After that setback at the end of May, it took Crochet three months just to be cleared to throw off the mound again.
Now that he’s been able to do so three times, and is scheduled for a fourth bullpen session at Fenway Park on Tuesday, there is legitimate hope he can be on the roster when the Red Sox open their postseason on Sept. 29 -- likely at Yankee Stadium.
This time, assuming he makes it back, Crochet will be cast in a much different role, but one that can still be impactful.
Figuring you have questions about how and when Crochet fits in, here are some answers.
Can Crochet make it back before the regular season ends?
It’s not impossible. His next key step after graduating from bullpen sessions will be to face hitters. That could happen as soon as this weekend, depending on what the club decides after Tuesday’s session.
Ideally, when it comes to Crochet’s situation, the Triple-A season would go a little longer. But, alas, it ends on Sunday.
It seems more likely Crochet will throw live batting practice and/or some type of simulated game rather than getting into a Minor League game, perhaps doing so multiple times.
Would this leave time for one tune-up before the regular season ends on Sept. 27? Perhaps, but not necessarily.
Would Crochet be thrown right into the fire of the playoffs?
What if there isn’t time for Crochet to pitch in any type of game setting before the Wild Card Series starts? Would the Red Sox still put him on the roster?
Well, if he’s throwing up to his capabilities, the answer is absolutely yes.
“It's Garrett Crochet,” said Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “If Garrett Crochet looks like Garrett Crochet and he's healthy and able to go out there and pitch, and it looks like him? Yeah, that helps any team.”
What would Boston’s bullpen cast look like with Crochet in the mix?
In a word, dominant. Through their first 150 games of the season entering Tuesday, Boston’s bullpen has a 3.11 ERA, best in the Majors. That’s without Crochet.
Now, add Crochet and possibly 2024 Tanner Houck, who is on a Minor League rehab assignment in his return from Tommy John surgery, and Tracy’s relief crew could have a succession of pitchers with nasty stuff.
At 38 years old, lefty Aroldis Chapman continues to be a force. He has one of the best eighth-inning setup men in the game in front of him in righty Garrett Whitlock. Tyron Guerrero, the righty with triple-digit heat, is due back in the next couple of days after missing the last couple of weeks with right shoulder inflammation. Power lefty Erik Miller has been tremendous since he was acquired at the Aug. 3 Trade Deadline.
Brayan Bello, who hasn’t had much success has a starter this season but has been largely stellar in relief, is another weapon. Add Crochet and Houck to those five pitchers and the Sox would have bullpen depth that would be the envy of most teams.
How would the Sox use Crochet?
The beauty of Crochet is that he could work out of a hybrid role, meaning he could be available for whichever part of the game Tracy needs him most.
Keep in mind that Crochet was a relief pitcher not just in college at Tennessee, but also for the White Sox before being converted to a starting role in ‘24. He has experience working in the early, middle and late part of games.
Thinking outside the box, the Sox could even deploy Crochet as an opener if the occasion called for it, given his experience starting games.
“He'd have plenty of comfort opening if you wanted to go that route," Tracy said. "He pitched out of the 'pen. So if you need him to come in the middle innings of a game, a two-inning pocket, I'm sure he'd have comfort doing that, too."

Boston Red Sox fans will not be seeing former top prospect Kristian Campbell in the big leagues at all this season, unfortunately.
On Tuesday, Tommy Cassell of the Worcester T&G Sports reported that Campbell's season is over. Campbell was placed on the seven-day Injured List due to a left foot contusion on Sep. 10. Cassell reported that Campbell will not be able to return before Triple-A Worcester's season ends on Sep. 20.
"Some injury updates today in AAA Worcester: Tanner Houck is scheduled to pitch one inning (20-25 pitches) in relief," Cassell wrote. "Romy Gonzalez is in at DH despite being a bit banged up. Iggy Suarez mentioned he's "an option" to contribute with the Red Sox moving forward. Kristian Campbell is out for the rest of the WooSox season. 'He was a big part of what we've been doing,' Suarez said. 'So, it's definitely a downer for that.'"
Kristian Campbell Is Done For The Year
That's some really unfortunate news for one of the most intriguing players in the Red Sox's system. Campbell made the big league club out of Spring Training in 2025 as the first member of the "Big 3," including him, Roman Anthony and Marcelo Mayer. He was red-hot out of the gate to the point that Boston handed him an eight-year, $60 million deal. But things took a turn afterward. Campbell was demoted to Triple-A in June, 2025. He hasn't been in the majors since.
Campbell played in 73 down in Triple-A last season and then didn't make the Red Sox's big league club out of camp. He has been down in the minors all season this year trying to work his way back.
The 24-year-old spent the season in the outfield as Boston tried to slow things down after moving him around all over the place last year. For Boston, it is loaded in the outfield to the point that there was a logjam early on in the season. Then, despite the Red Sox losing Roman Anthony to the Injured List for a while, there still wasn't space for Campbell in the majors.
Overall, Campbell wrapped up his season after playing in 109 games for Triple-A and slashing .256/.383/.380 with a .763 OPS, eight homers and 51 RBIs. Hopefully, he's able to get back on track and get back into the mix by the time Spring Training rolls around. Who could've seen this coming back in 2025? Campbell looked like a franchise cornerstone piece. Unfortunately, he hasn't been in the majors in over a year and now that won't be happening this year.

ARLINGTON -- Right-handed reliever Justin Slaten’s season is over, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy announced ahead of Boston’s three-game series opener against the Rangers at Globe Life Field on Tuesday night.
According to Tracy, Slaten met with Dr. Keith Meister, an orthopedist in the Dallas area, and an evaluation revealed “degenerative changes in his flexor mass” in his right elbow.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is [a platelet-rich plasma injection]. He’s going to rehab and go from there, but because of that, it’s going to probably cost him the season.”
“As we sit here right now, we were operating and moving forward, planning on having to operate without him,” Tracy said. “This maybe adds some finality to the fact that, ‘OK, now the chances of getting him back are slim.’”
The 29-year-old Slaten posted a 4.60 ERA with 39 strikeouts across 31 1/3 innings over 36 appearances for Boston.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said. “At least now the finality of knowing we can’t have him back. But you guys have seen the way he can come in and pitch in those big-moment cleanup innings, to get you out of the sixth, seventh inning. We’ve seen him do that, so he’s an important arm. But we have to deal with it and move on.”
Slaten and Garrett Whitlock served as the Sox’s top right-handed setup men when both went down last month. Whitlock returned from the IL on Aug. 29.
When Slaten and Whitlock first went down, Tracy believed he had enough arms to navigate the bullpen. That depth, however, continues to be tested.
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, who landed on the IL on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation, was expected to be activated Wednesday but experienced muscle cramping in his lower back Tuesday, delaying his return. According to Tracy, the team does not know when Guerrero will be activated.

The Boston Red Sox have four series between them and the postseason, which they are all but certain to make. The Tampa Bay Rays and New York Yankees have already clinched their spots and the Red Sox shouldn't be far behind.
They don't have an easy final two weeks ahead, however. Boston will face either a playoff team or playoff hopefuls during the home stretch and they'll be just as hungry as the Sox are to clinch their spot, maintain their standing or improve it.
The final four series begin with the Texas Rangers, who have the American League's third Wild Card spot in their sights — they sit half a game behind the Toronto Blue Jays, the first team out, before their September 15 series opener against Boston. Texas should be playing some of its best baseball with a playoff berth on the line, but the Red Sox have a secret weapon on their side to try and take it off its game: Wilyer Abreu.
The outfielder's success against the Rangers verges on "ownership." Over 17 games against Texas in his career, Abreu is slashing .436/.484/1.018 with five doubles, nine home runs and 22 RBI.
Wilyer Abreu's success against Rangers could be a huge difference maker for Red Sox at the perfect time
His dominance over Texas began in August 2024, Abreu's rookie season, when he hit three homers in one series against it, including a two-homer game. He logged two more two-home run games against the Rangers in 2025 (Opening Day and May 7).
Abreu plays particularly well at Globe Life Field, the Rangers' home ballpark and where they'll face the Sox from September 15-17 for their season series finale. The 27-year-old boasts a shocking 2.035 OPS through eight appearances in Arlington, Texas, and the Red Sox would certainly love him to carry their offense enough to clinch a playoff berth this series.
Boston has some tough pitching matchups ahead, including a potential series-opening date with Jacob deGrom (3.80 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 186 strikeouts in 149.1 innings pitched) (subscription required). It's also scheduled to face former Washington Nationals starter MacKenzie Gore and possibly Nathan Eovaldi, though the schedule isn't yet confirmed. Eovaldi and Gore haven't been as successful this year as they have in the past, but Eovaldi presents a challenge every time he takes the mound.
Abreu's success against the Rangers hasn't yet reached Rafael Devers-Yankees-Gerrit Cole territory (and it might never feel as good since the Yankees are the Yankees), but he's inching closer with every series. Maybe the yearly two-home run game at Globe Life Field comes right on time to lift the Red Sox into postseason certainty.

Over the last few weeks, the Boston Red Sox have gotten positive updates left and right about injured starting pitchers.
First and foremost, Garrett Crochet has been throwing and is trending towards a late-season return in Boston's bullpen, barring a setback. Tanner Houck has been on a minor league rehab assignment and is trending up. Plus, the current expectation is that Johan Oviedo is nearing a minor league rehab assignment as well. Now, it sounds like another hurler is trending up as well. On Tuesday, Tommy Cassell of the Worcester T&G Sports reported that there have been "some rumblings" that Kutter Crawford could join Triple-A Worcester throughout the week as well.
"And there are some rumblings that Kutter Crawford could be in Worcester this week, too," Cassell wrote. "The 30-year-old righty has been sidelined since March with right wrist and forearm issues and made one rehab stint with Worcester on April 11 before being shut down again. Crawford hasn’t been confirmed yet whether he will pitch in Worcester."
Kutter Crawford Is Trending Up
How about that?
Crawford hasn't been talked about in a long time. Now, it seems like the righty could potentially be in Worcester this week. Things move quickly in baseball, to say the least.
Crawford missed the entire 2025 season and he was trending up at one point early in the 2026 season and even went on a rehab assignment with Triple-A Worcester, although he suffered a setback and has been on the shelf ever since.
Now, of course, this doesn't guarantee that he will help the Red Sox before the 2026 season comes to a close. In fact, it arguably would be surprising to see him on the Red Sox's roster before the season comes to a close. Crawford's last appearance in a game was on April 11, 2026 with Worcester. When he does take the mound again, he's going to have to build up and get the rust off. The regular season will end for the Red Sox in just 12 days, as of writing, on Sep. 27. That's not a lot of time to begin a rehab assignment for the first time in five months and return to the majors with the playoffs looming.
But it's still good news in general for Boston. What if Crawford does pitch this week for Triple-A Worcester and looks like a game-changer? Maybe, he could surprise. Even if he doesn't, he's under team control for the 2027 and 2028 seasons. If the Red Sox could enter Spring Training with Crawford as a legit candidte for either the rotation — or even the bullpen — that makes the team better. Or, if he proves he's healthy, maybe he could even be an intriguing trade chip this winter.
All in all, hearing that one of the Red Sox's hurlers are trending up after missing so much time is positive in itself.

item.content:encoded:
Cam Schlittler brought his A-game on Sunday. Facing the Mets in the rubber game of the Subway Series at Yankee Stadium, the Yankees’ fireballer was nearly untouchable over the course of six scoreless innings, striking out eight while allowing just one hit, a fifth-inning double by Brett Baty. Meanwhile in Baltimore, the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease worked around five walks to allow just one run over five innings while striking out nine. The two righties are engaged in an intriguing race for the AL Cy Young Award, one that could go down to the wire. The NL race is a tight one as well, with the Brewers’ Jacob Misiorowski the favorite but hardly the only one under consideration.
The 25-year-old Schlittler and 24-year-old Misiorowski are undeniably the frontrunners in their respective leagues, from both statistical and narrative standpoints. They lead in our Tom Tango-modeled Cy Young projections, and as of mid-August, they dominated polls taken by MLB.com. Nonetheless, the statistical races that can influence both our perceptions and voter behavior aren’t entirely decided, and with less than two weeks to go in the regular season, the races are worth a closer look.
The 6-foot-7 Misiorowski and 6-foot-6 Schlittler share similarities beyond their impressive heights. Both are in their first full major league seasons, after arriving in mid-2025 and helping their teams to the playoffs while showing poise beyond their years; this October, they’ll be seasoned postseason veterans. They’re the majors’ two hardest-throwing starters, with Misiorowski breaking velocity records all over the place. His average four-seam velocity — a mind-blowing 100.6 mph — not only leads the majors, but it’s also the fastest single-season velocity by a starter in the pitch-tracking era (from 2008 onward), hardly surprising given that he owns the (scrolling, scrolling, scrolling) 117 fastest pitches by a starter in pitch-tracking history — including a record-setting 105.5-mph heater to the Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 26 — and 353 of the 394 pitches of at least 102 mph thrown by a starter. Hunter Greene is the only other one in double digits (12). Schlittler merely ranks second among all starters this year, with an average velocity of 98.0 mph, which is still good for fifth in the pitch-tracking era.
Both righties have other exceptional offerings that test the adage “man cannot live by fastball alone,” in that Misiorowski’s cutter and Schlittler’s sinker are their second-most valuable pitches according to Statcast. But whatever they’re throwing, they’re dominating. Each leads his respective league in ERA (1.95 for both) and fWAR (6.0 for Misiorowski, 5.9 for Schlittler), with the Yankee additionally leading the AL in starts (31), innings (184 2/3), strikeout-walk differential (25.5%), and bWAR (7.1), and the Brewer leading the NL in strikeouts (236), strikeout rate (38.3%), and FIP (2.24). That ought to be enough to hand out the hardware, right?
Quite possibly, but not all of those statistical leads is insurmountable. Zooming in for a closer look first at the AL, Schlittler and Cease have separated themselves from the pack more so than they have from each other:
| Pitcher | W | L | GS | IP | K% | BB% | K-BB% | HR/9 | ERA | xERA | FIP | fWAR | bWAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cam Schlittler | 14 | 6 | 31 | 184.2 | 31.6% | 6.1% | 25.5% | 0.78 | 1.95 | 2.88 | 2.57 | 5.9 | 7.1 |
| Dylan Cease | 11 | 5 | 28 | 166.1 | 35.3% | 10.8% | 24.6% | 0.60 | 2.38 | 2.81 | 2.48 | 5.6 | 6.0 |
| Parker Messick | 11 | 9 | 29 | 172.1 | 26.0% | 6.9% | 19.1% | 0.84 | 2.51 | 3.07 | 3.11 | 4.5 | 5.7 |
| Drew Rasmussen | 14 | 5 | 28 | 160.1 | 25.6% | 4.3% | 21.3% | 0.79 | 2.81 | 3.11 | 2.88 | 4.6 | 3.9 |
| Sonny Gray | 17 | 5 | 27 | 156.2 | 22.0% | 6.6% | 15.4% | 0.86 | 2.76 | 3.84 | 3.46 | 3.2 | 4.0 |
I couldn’t fit it in the table, but Schlittler is third in strikeouts (228) behind Cease (236) and Gavin Williams (235), whose run prevention numbers (3.78 ERA, 3.49 FIP) rule him out here. (Dan Szymborski has a closer look at Williams’ breakout up today.) Messick, Rasmussen, and Gray have all authored fine seasons, but none has a compelling enough statistical case to elevate him into the company of the top two; win totals and winning percentage don’t cut it these days. The ability of Schlittler and Cease to miss bats separates them in value from the rest of the group, both via our FIP-driven WAR and Baseball Reference’s version, where they don’t have to share as much credit (or blame) with their fielders given the lower rates of balls in play. More on that subject in a moment.
With Gerrit Cole scuffling late in his first season after returning from Tommy John surgery, and Max Fried limited to 18 starts by a bone bruise in his elbow, Schlittler has emerged as the Yankees’ bona fide ace and as one of the league’s true workhorses. Six other AL pitchers have made at least 30 starts so far, but only Michael Wacha has thrown at least 180 innings; he’s at 182 2/3, and while Tanner Bibee (177 1/3), Reid Detmers (174), Williams (174) and a couple others may get there, they won’t catch Schlittler. Nineteen of Schlittler’s starts have been quality starts, the league’s second-highest total behind Wacha (20); Cease is tied for eighth with 15. Schlittler has either put up zeroes or allowed just one run in 22 starts, including each of his last seven. Sixteen of those zero-or-one-run starts have lasted at least six innings; Gray and Rasmussen are among those tied for second with 13, while Cease is tied for sixth with 12. Beyond the aforementioned categories in which he’s led the league, Schlittler is second to Cease in FIP and xERA by less than one-tenth of a run, with the third-highest strikeout rate and sixth-lowest walk rate.
Cease, whom the Blue Jays signed to a seven-year, $210 million deal this past winter, has bounced back from an uneven 2025 performance with the Padres, one in which he put up a 4.54 ERA and a 3.56 FIP. He’s been every bit as good as the Blue Jays could have hoped for, something that can’t be said for many players on the defending AL champions. He has totaled seven starts of at least six innings with zero runs allowed, tied for third in the majors behind Cristopher Sánchez (10) and Rasmussen (eight); Schlittler is tied for seventh with six.
Cease has been the most unhittable starter in the AL, with the lowest batting average allowed (.177) and fewest hits per nine (5.68). He chalked up the first no-hitter of his career in 2024 while pitching for the Padres, and has flirted with a second one on a couple occasions this season. He tossed eight hitless innings on July 8 against the Giants at Oracle Park before allowing a single to Heliot Ramos to start the ninth, at which point he departed, having thrown 118 pitches in what was by then a 10-0 rout; days later, he was named to start the All-Star Game for the AL. He pitched 6 2/3 hitless innings against the Yankees on August 22 in the Bronx before allowing back-to-back singles to Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Austin Wells, and additionally threw a one-hit shutout against the Red Sox at Fenway Park on July 25, with a fifth-inning double by Andruw Monasterio the lone blemish.
Both Schlittler and Cease have averaged a hair under six innings per start (5.96 for the former, 5.94 for the latter). The difference in innings totals comes down to Cease’s having spent 15 days on the injured list for a mild hamstring strain starting in late May.
Cease has the higher strikeout rate, but also the higher walk rate — the highest among AL qualifiers, in fact — but even with that, his FIP and xERA are slightly better than Schlittler’s. Those estimators are defense-independent, but it’s worth noting the defenses behind the two pitchers. Statcast, which tracks the individual Fielding Run Values accumulated behind each pitcher, shows Cease with slightly more support, with his fielders putting up 7 FRV behind him compared to 5 FRV for Schlittler. The bWAR calculations, which start with actual runs allowed per nine innings with a variety of adjustments for defense, opposing offenses, and park factors, credit Cease with having the better defense behind him (based on team-level Defensive Runs Saved), worth 0.24 runs per nine to Schlittler’s 0.09 runs per nine. In other words, by that reckoning Cease shares more credit with his fielders, though that difference is canceled out by adjustments for his facing better offenses and pitching in a higher-scoring environment.
In the end, Schlittler’s combination of superior run prevention, better peripherals, and a larger innings load separates him from Cease by 1.1 bWAR and 0.3 fWAR. Depending upon where you fall on the spectrum of factoring in defense, it’s somewhere between a narrow margin and a substantial one, but either way it lines up with the consensus. Barring a blowup over his final couple of starts, Schlittler looks like the right call for the AL Cy Young.
The NL race isn’t as clear-cut:
| Pitcher | W | L | GS | IP | K% | BB% | K-BB% | HR/9 | ERA | xERA | FIP | fWAR | bWAR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jacob Misiorowski | 14 | 5 | 27 | 161.1 | 38.3% | 6.7% | 31.7% | 0.78 | 1.95 | 2.10 | 2.24 | 6.0 | 5.6 |
| Cristopher Sánchez | 17 | 5 | 30 | 187.1 | 27.0% | 5.4% | 21.6% | 0.77 | 2.79 | 3.31 | 2.72 | 5.8 | 7.6 |
| Chris Sale | 14 | 9 | 26 | 157.0 | 30.3% | 4.9% | 25.4% | 0.52 | 2.18 | 3.05 | 2.29 | 5.7 | 5.5 |
| Jesús Luzardo | 14 | 5 | 29 | 178.2 | 29.4% | 8.8% | 20.7% | 0.76 | 2.87 | 2.85 | 2.78 | 5.5 | 6.4 |
On a pure rate basis, the numbers favor Misiorowski. Not only does he lead the NL in the half-dozen categories highlighted above, but he’s been even more unhittable than Cease, with a .155 batting average allowed and 4.91 hits per nine given up, both tops in the majors among qualifiers. But because he’s worked in a six-man rotation all season long, and has been kept on a slightly shorter leash — averaging 5.97 innings per start to Sale’s 6.04, Luzardo’s 6.14, and Sánchez’s 6.24 — he has thrown 26 fewer innings than Sánchez.
The results have generally been dazzling. Misiorowski has 10 starts with double-digit strikeout totals, second in the majors only to Williams; Cease has nine, Luzardo six, Sánchez five, Sale and Schlittler four. The Miz has six scoreless starts of at least six innings, including a 15-strikeout one-hit shutout against the Phillies on June 12, marred only by a fourth-inning Kyle Schwarber single. But even with a majors-leading 236 strikeouts, the innings total puts him at a slight disadvantage in some contexts. Misiorowski is tied for fifth in the league with 18 quality starts, with Sánchez tied for second (20) alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto, one behind Sandy Alcantara; Sale is fourth with 19, Luzardo tied for ninth with 17. Misiorowski’s total of 11 starts of at least six innings with no more than one run allowed trails Sánchez (13), as well as Luzardo and Sale (12 apiece).
Sánchez has the volume advantage. Working with a sinker that averages “only” 95.0 mph — offset by one of the game’s best changeups — he’s reached the 200-strikeout plateau for the second consecutive season; his 212 ranks third behind Misiorowski and Luzado (221). His strikeout rate ranks seventh, his walk rate third, his strikeout-walk differential fourth, behind Misiorowski, Sale, and Luzardo in that order. He made a huge impression earlier this season by reeling off a streak of 50 2/3 scoreless innings in May, the longest ever by a lefty, and the fifth longest of all time; not since Orel Hershiser’s 59-inning streak in 1988 broke Don Drysdale’s record had anyone reached 50. That streak helped Sánchez land the honor of starting the All-Star Game for the NL, though Misiorowski’s workload — he was scheduled to start on the Sunday before the game, officially ruling him out for the honor, and then was scratched from that outing due to arm fatigue — played a part. Even then, Sánchez’s 2.62 ERA was a full run per nine higher than Misiorowski’s. On that note, Sánchez has a 3.15 ERA and a 3.46 FIP since the break, though by FIP (2.70 before, 2.77 after), he’s been basically the same pitcher, and even his xERAs (3.24 before, 3.46 after) are closer than his actual ones.
The 37-year-old Sale has thrown even fewer innings than Misiorowski because he’s been given some extra rest between starts. It’s a choice that’s paid off handsomely for the Braves and for the pitcher, who cracked 100 mph on a pitch on August 27, his fastest since 2018, and who has been positively brilliant in the second half, with a 2.14 ERA and a 1.41 FIP, the latter thanks to a combination of a 32.6% strikeout rate, a 2.7% walk rate, and 0.15 homers per nine.
According to Statcast, Sale has gotten the best defensive support of this quartet at 5 FRV, ahead of Sánchez (3), Misiorowski (0), and Luzardo (-3). That defense has helped to offset Sale’s having an xERA almost a run higher than the Miz. The two are on nearly even footing in the grand scheme, but based on their performances to date, I don’t see anything that would elevate Sale past Misiorowski except some sentiment for the old guy, a likely future Hall of Famer.
As for Luzardo, there’s not much separating him from Sánchez. Though his season hasn’t been as eye-catching, it’s been stellar, but in the wake of his two-hit, 12-strikeout shutout against the Braves on September 7, he’s dealt with shoulder stiffness and inflammation. Thanks to a clean MRI, he’s avoided the injured list so far, though he did have a turn skipped, and it wouldn’t be surprising if his workload between here and October is dialed down.
The two Phillies have had to survive playing in front of the team’s notoriously lousy defense. Sánchez has the highest BABIP among NL qualifiers (.335), 41 points ahead of the seventh-ranked Luzardo (.294) and 101 points ahead of Misiorowski (.234). Where Statcast tracks the individual FRVs behind each pitcher, Baseball Reference’s WAR adjustments are at the team level, which may be heavy-handed for pitchers who differ in groundball/fly ball orientation. Sanchez’s 58.2% groundball rate leads the league, while Luzardo’s 48.3% is seventh; both are more dependent upon the team’s shaky infield than its more middling (but still not good) outfield. In the bWAR calculations, there’s about half a run per nine difference between those two (-0.24 for Luzardo, -0.26 for Sánchez) and the other pair (0.24 for Misiorowski, 0.27 for Sale). The latter duo Phillies pair also gets favorable adjustments for pitching in tougher ballparks (which are tracked individually). The adjustments give the two Phillies the higher bWARs, with Sánchez having the edge.
I think the overall choice comes down to Sánchez’s advantage in volume versus Misiorowski’s edge in dominance, and for some voters or otherwise interested observers, that steers it into subjective and/or aesthetic territory. I can understand favoring the guy at the vanguard of extreme velocity — not just because of the raw velo, but also for what he’s done with it in terms of unhittability and sheer brilliance — but I can also appreciate the impulse to reward a throwback, particularly one working under the adverse conditions of being backed by Trea Turner (-16 DRS, -10 FRV) and Alec Bohm (-8 DRS, -5 FRV). Based on their numbers to this point, I’d vote Misiorowski, but I’d hardly blame anyone for choosing Sánchez. Nevertheless, I suspect his second-half fade has probably doomed him to another second-place finish.
Brooklyn-based Jay Jaffe is a senior writer for FanGraphs, the author of The Cooperstown Casebook (Thomas Dunne Books, 2017) and the creator of the JAWS (Jaffe WAR Score) metric for Hall of Fame analysis. He founded the Futility Infielder website (2001), was a columnist for Baseball Prospectus (2005-2012) and a contributing writer for Sports Illustrated (2012-2018). He has been a recurring guest on MLB Network and a member of the BBWAA since 2011, and a Hall of Fame voter since 2021. Follow him on BlueSky @jayjaffe.bsky.social.

Wherever Needed, Garrett Whitlock Open to Helping Red Sox in Rotation or Bullpen originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Red Sox have thrived this season thanks to clutch hitting and a reliable pitching staff. The bullpen has also held things down, from Aroldis Chapman closing games to Garrett Whitlock being used wherever needed.
Whitlock has worked as a starter and a reliever throughout his career. He is willing to do whatever it takes to help the Red Sox. That includes another potential crack at the rotation.
Selected by the Red Sox in the Rule 5 Draft in 2020, Whitlock started in relief and has been in and out of the rotation. He has suffered several injuries but that hasn't stopped him from producing.
In 2024, Whitlock posted a 1.96 ERA in four games as a starter. In 2025, he had a 2.25 ERA in 62 appearances in he bullpen.
This season, Whitlock has pitched in 49.2 innings. He appeared on the injured list between May and June and returned from an elbow issue. A spot in the rotation may not be available, but when healthy, he can fill in wherever needed.
"I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it's definitely something I'd be open to. Will I?" Whitlock said via The Boston Globe. "I'm not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's] office and be like, 'Hey, I'm starting.'
"So it's one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it's something I'd always be open to."
Whitlock played in 13 games in July, a month where the Red Sox won 15 straight games. He went 12.1 innings, striking out 10 while owning a 0.73 ERA. After owning an 1.80 ERA in August, he hasn't given up a run in four September appearances, striking out seven batters.
The workhorse's efforts helped propel the Red Sox to the second Wild Card spot with just a few games to go before the playoffs begin.
Whitlock has two club options on his contract. Thriving as a reliever, Whitlock will look at all options, especially if the Red Sox come to him with ideas to improve the team.
"We're pretty good on starting depth," Whitlock said. "If I become a free agent and a team approaches me about it, I'm open to it and see how it goes."

Payton Tolle. Ranger Suarez. Sonny Gray.
The Boston Red Sox don’t have to think very long about what their starting rotation should look like for their inevitable wild card matchup with the New York Yankees.
I’ll go and find the numbers to back up this opinion, but before we dive into those let’s just all acknowledge the oldest factor in the book when it comes to these kinds of decisions: the eye test.
Tolle has been a man possessed since the start of August, with seven of his eight outings across that stretch being quality starts and just three of those starts ending before he completed six innings — 48.0 innings pitched, 13 earned runs, 63 strikeouts, 11 walks issued, 2.44 ERA, 2.37 FIP, and one Immaculate Inning.
Suarez shut me right the hell up since your boy had the bright idea of publicly pointing out that he tends to struggle in the month of September. He put up a 4.00 ERA across 168.2 innings pitched in that month throughout the first eight seasons of his career. He’s got a 0.64 across his two starts this month, which isn’t exactly the same sample size but he has been dealing when it matters most.
Gray has also been really good, but he’s clearly starting to strain after carrying the rotation on his back for the majority of the season. The one start he made after receiving extra days rest was superb (7.0 IP, 0R, W). His las start, on normal rest, was rather pedestrian, like the few before he got the breather (6.0, 3R, L).
If you want to talk about how the trio best flows together, it is also important to note where the game is being played and who they’ll be playing against. The Yankees just aren’t as good when they have to deploy their righty-heavy lineup, as it forces guys like Amed Rosario and Heliot Ramos into games over Luis Garcia and Ryan McMahon, and helps limit the overall effectiveness of Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, and Jazz Chisholm Jr.
Yankee Stadium has been home to 18 home runs given up by left-handed starting pitchers and 41 home runs given up by right-handed starting pitchers in 2026. If that’s not enough to influence your decision, what is?
Is it the fact that Tolle has the smallest book out on him and has gotten better in August and September? Is it the fact that Suarez has the best postseason pedigree of the three? Is it the fact that Gray notoriously hasn’t pitched well in The Bronx?
I don’t know, man. Tolle in Game 1 of the ALDS sounds pretty damn good to me…

Being the longest-tenured pitcher on the Red Sox staff has been a lonely role for Garrett Whitlock this year, and one he is eager to hand back to its rightful owner.
The right-hander has been elite in his sixth big-league season, all with Boston. Whitlock entered Monday’s off-day with a 1.81 ERA, 31.2 strikeout percentage and 3.8 walk percentage, all career bests, through 51 appearances, with 58 strikeouts and just seven walks in 49 2/3 innings.
On Monday, Whitlock was announced as the Red Sox nominee for Major League Baseball’s prestigious Roberto Clemente Award, “bestowed annually to the player who best represents the game of baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions, both on and off the field.”
But Whitlock has spent most of his excellent campaign without his closest friend on the team: fellow righty Tanner Houck, who spent most of the season down at the club’s Fort Myers, Fla., spring training complex, rehabbing from his August 2025 Tommy John surgery.
Which meant that for the first time in half a decade, Whitlock and Houck celebrated their June birthdays – they each turned 30 on the 11th and 29th, respectively – apart. They typically play card or board games, cribbage and euchre are among their favorites, and get ice cream with their wives.
“We always do something to celebrate, hang out at each other’s apartments or houses, and everything,” Whitlock told the Herald. “So it was weird not having that this year. And so yeah, it’s nice to have my best friend back.”
Houck finally returned to Boston at the start of the last homestand, then began a rehab assignment in the minor leagues. He is on track to rejoin the Red Sox for the tail-end of the regular season, and for what they hope will be the team’s first deep playoff run since 2021, when he and Whitlock were the rookies of the pitching staff.
“So good to have him back,” Whitlock said. “Love seeing him in the locker room, and the guys love having him around. So excited for him to get back with us soon.”
Whitlock is eager to return the title of longest-tenured Red Sox player to Houck when he returns to the active roster. Tuesday marks the six-year anniversary of Houck’s MLB debut. Whitlock arrived several months later via the Rule 5 Draft, and debuted at the start of the 2021 season. Together, the two righties have ridden the highest of highs and lowest of lows in the years since: a stunningly successful 2021 season, their respective season-ending surgeries in 2022, Whitlock’s season-ending elbow surgery in May 2024, and Houck’s last summer. Houck supported Whitlock through the sudden death of his younger brother, Gavrie, in 2023, and celebrated when Whitlock became a father in the summer of 2024.
“It’s huge,” Whitlock said of his relationship with Houck. “Everyone’s left, and we’re still here. … We’ve been through everything together, through all the changes, whether it’s front office changes, coaching staff changes, our health changes, literally everything.
“It’s been one of those things that we’ve been through so much together that just grows your friendship, and so it’s nice to have a familiar face back around, and my best friend on the team, and I’m looking forward to sharing the rest of the year with him.”
The Red Sox plan to use Houck in a relief role, which will put him and Whitlock in the bullpen together for the first time since 2022.
“He’s got elite stuff,” Whitlock said. “You saw when he was the closer in ‘22, how good his stuff is. And so I’m excited for – I think people were writing him off before he had surgery, and I’m excited for people to see Tanner be Tanner again. And I think as soon as he shows that, people will start coming back and loving him again, and it’ll be great to have that.”
Whitlock and Houck are the only active pitchers in the organization who know what it’s like to play a postseason home game at Fenway Park. (Boston’s lone playoff appearance since was last year’s three-game wild card series, all of which played out at Yankee Stadium.)
“It was a crazy ride,” Whitlock recalled of 2021. “The whole thing was surreal, because rookie year, I never even expected to be there. So it was surreal, and loved every second of it, and want some more. We’re ready to get back.”
Though some may scoff at the importance of such experience, many Red Sox players and opponents know that October at Fenway is a whole other animal. Whitlock, and, he hopes, Houck are looking forward to sharing their experience with younger teammates.
“I think the biggest thing I will tell them is, don’t change what’s gotten you here,” Whitlock said. “So many times, people try and do so many different things, in the playoffs and pressure situations, and it’s like, you can’t do that.
“You’ve got to do exactly what brought you to these moments, because it worked. It worked to get you there. It worked to get you to these moments, and so you can’t try and do more. You can’t try and change anything. Keep doing exactly what you’ve been doing, because what got you here is good enough to get you through it.”
But first, the Red Sox must punch their ticket. They entered Monday’s off-day with their magic number down to six.
“Those conversations haven’t really started just quite yet, because it’s like, alright, we still got some work to do to get to the playoffs,” Whitlock said. “Hopefully the closer we get, those will start picking up.
“But I’m excited. We’re at the door, so we just need to finish our job, and get in.”
